title: The tongue (James 3:1–12)
hookLine: a small rudder, a small spark: the tongue sets forests on fire

cards: A wildfire can start from almost nothing. A spark from a dragged chain. One cigarette.
A campfire left smoldering. A few days later the smoke is visible from space, and whole towns are packing their cars.
Investigators sometimes trace the fire back to a single point on the ground, small enough to cover with your hand.
James never saw a satellite photo, but he knew what a small fire can do, and he used it to describe something that sits in every mouth.

teach.b: He starts with a warning to teachers. Not many of you should become teachers, he says, because teachers will be judged more strictly. People who talk for a living have more to answer for.
Then three pictures of small things steering big ones. A bit in a horse's mouth turns the whole animal.

teach.h: A BIT, A RUDDER, A SPARK.
teach.b: A huge ship, driven by fierce winds, is "turned about with a very small helm," the rudder, wherever the pilot wants.

And then: "Even so the tongue is a little member, and boasteth great things. Behold, how great a matter a little fire kindleth!" That word matter is a puzzle in English. The Greek word means wood, or forest.
How great a forest a small fire sets ablaze. The bit and the rudder steer. The spark destroys.
Then something that stings: people have tamed every kind of animal, birds and snakes and sea creatures, "But the tongue can no man tame; it is an unruly evil, full of deadly poison."
And the line that turns it inward: "Out of the same mouth proceedeth blessing and cursing. My brethren, these things ought not so to be."
With the tongue, James says, we bless God, and with it we curse people made in God's likeness. Praise on Sunday, cursing by Monday. Does a spring pour fresh water and bitter from the same opening?
Can a fig tree grow olives? He isn't saying never speak.

teach.h: HOW GREAT A MATTER A LITTLE FIRE KINDLETH!
teach.b: He's saying words are fire. They can warm a house or burn it down, and the same mouth does both.

how: Some Christians include their speech in a daily or weekly self-examination, and churches turn to James 3 when teaching about gossip, anger and online behavior.

a person's taste for rich food and drink
a small part of us that can steer or burn

the Greek word means wood or forest.

games.q: James asks: can a spring pour out fresh and bitter water from the same opening? what's his point?
o: blessing God and cursing people from one mouth ought not to be.
games.why: "Out of the same mouth proceedeth blessing and cursing. My brethren, these things ought not so to be."

practice: Think back to the last unkind thing you said, out loud or in a text, and without punishing yourself, picture it like a spark landing in dry grass.

Then picture the moment today you're most likely to say something sharp, and your mouth staying closed, or opening with something else after a breath. If you pray, you can ask for a guard on your mouth.

wordCard.voice: The tongue. For James, a small part of the body that steers like a rudder and burns like a spark, and that no one can fully tame.

orig.note: Greek: tongue, and also language. the word behind 'the tongue' all through James 3.
